title: Indian Producers Eye Cyprus as Film Scheme Offers Rebate of up to 45 Per Cent
excerpt: India's High Commissioner met producer Jitendra Mishra in Nicosia to discuss joint productions and Indian cinema screenings, as Cyprus courts Bollywood with cash rebates, tax credits and VAT refunds — and its first Bollywood feature, Ishqa, is already in the pipeline.
body:
• India's High Commissioner to Cyprus, Manish, met film producer Jitendra Mishra in Nicosia to discuss joint film productions, special screenings of Indian cinema in Cyprus and opportunities for young filmmakers, Cyprus Mail reported on Tuesday.
  • The draw for Indian producers is Cyprus's film scheme: a cash rebate of up to 45 per cent on eligible expenditure in Cyprus, set by a cultural assessment, with tax credits, equipment-investment deductions and VAT refunds also available.
  • The first Bollywood feature to shoot in Cyprus, the romantic dramedy Ishqa, was announced in May; its makers said the incentives played an important part in the decision.
  • The talks were exploratory — no new production agreement or investment was announced.

Cyprus is making its pitch to Indian filmmakers, and the offer starts with money back. India's High Commissioner to Cyprus, Manish, met producer Jitendra Mishra in Nicosia to discuss joint film productions, special screenings of Indian cinema in Cyprus and opportunities for young filmmakers to work with international professionals, Cyprus Mail reported on Tuesday. Manish described the meeting in a post on his personal social media account and encouraged Indian filmmakers to explore the island's locations and incentives.

"The meeting was exploratory: no new film production agreement or investment was announced."

Mishra is a producer with a long record in children's and socially themed cinema: he is president of the International Centre of Films for Children and Young People (CIFEJ), festival director of the Smile International Film Festival for Children and Youth, an associate producer of I Am Kalam and producer of The Last Color. He has been involved in the production, distribution and promotion of more than 100 films and is a recipient of India's National Film Award. In Nicosia, he offered to help build contacts between Indian and Cypriot film professionals and to explore special screenings, including award-winning regional films and films on education, social inclusion and women's empowerment. The meeting was exploratory: no new film production agreement or investment was announced.

The incentive: up to 45 per cent back

Under the film scheme administered through Invest Cyprus, qualifying productions can choose a cash rebate of up to 45 per cent of eligible expenditure incurred in Cyprus, with the exact amount set by the production's score in a cultural test. The rebate is paid once filming is completed, after an audit report is reviewed by the Cyprus Film Commission. As an alternative, producers can take a tax credit against corporate tax liability, and the scheme also offers tax deductions on investments in equipment and infrastructure and VAT refunds on qualifying expenditure. Feature films, television series, documentaries and animation are among the qualifying categories. For Cyprus, the return on a foreign shoot is local work: camera crews, technicians, accommodation, transport and equipment suppliers.

Ishqa: the first Bollywood feature

The courtship already has one result. In May, during President Nikos Christodoulides's visit to Mumbai, plans were announced for Ishqa, a romantic dramedy by Indian writer, director and producer Anjali Bhushan Mago with Cypriot filmmaker Athena Xenidou of Ray Films — set to be the first Bollywood feature shot in Cyprus. According to Invest Cyprus, the production submitted its application for filming permits in May 2026. Planned locations include Nicosia, Lefkara, Paphos, Protaras and Ayia Napa, and Mago said Cyprus's financial incentives played an important part in the decision. In June, Indian filmmakers met officials in Protaras to discuss locations and tourism infrastructure.

A wider cultural push

The film talks sit inside a broader cultural programme. Nicosia hosted the second International CIFEJ Symposium on November 16 and 17, covering children's cinema, film education and new technologies including artificial intelligence, and an October–November screening programme in the capital included the Indian films I Am Kalam and the short Little Big Dreams. Cypriot director Myrsini Aristidou's Hold Onto Me is screening at the 57th International Film Festival of India in Goa, running November 20 to 28, for its Indian premiere. The two governments have signed a cultural cooperation agreement covering 2026 to 2030, following Christodoulides's state visit to India in May, and are preparing to mark 65 years of diplomatic relations in 2027, with film festivals, screenings and filmmaker exchanges under discussion.
